content: This recommendation is conditional and based on low-certainty evidence. Similarly, hepatitis C virus (HCV) self-testing should be offered as an additional option to existing HCV testing services, supported by a strong recommendation and moderate-certainty evidence. COVID-19 self-testing using SARS-CoV-2 antigen-detecting rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) should also be made available as a complementary approach to professionally administered testing services, with a strong recommendation but low-certainty evidence. Pregnancy self-testing should be provided as an additional option for individuals seeking pregnancy testing, alongside health worker-led testing, supported by a strong recommendation but very low-certainty evidence. Self-collection of samples for gonorrhea and chlamydia testing should be made available as an additional approach to sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing services, supported by a strong recommendation and moderate-certainty evidence. Human papillomavirus (HPV) self-sampling should also be offered as an additional method for cervical cancer screening in individuals aged 30–60 years, supported by a strong recommendation and moderate-certainty evidence. The World Health Organization (WHO) has introduced a new 2023 recommendation suggesting that syphilis self-testing be offered as an additional approach to syphilis testing. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. Opportunities to expand or integrate syphilis self-testing into existing services should be prioritized. Evidence from a systematic review indicates that syphilis self-testing improves the uptake of syphilis testing, particularly among key populations such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, and transgender individuals. A meta-analysis of two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) demonstrated a more than fourfold increase in syphilis testing uptake when self-testing was available compared to standard laboratory-based testing. However, syphilis self-testing may not significantly affect the proportion of reactive test results or linkage to care compared to standard testing. Most individuals can correctly perform syphilis self-tests, although some users experience challenges with sample collection, particularly finger-pricking and transferring blood to the test cassette. Despite these challenges, no evidence suggests that user difficulties compromise test accuracy. Syphilis self-testing is generally well-accepted and considered desirable due to its convenience, privacy, and time-saving nature. Many users prefer blood-based self-tests over oral fluid tests, as they trust the results more. To optimize implementation, programs should address gaps in awareness about self-testing and STIs, provide clear instructions, and offer support tools such as videos, demonstrations, and peer assistance. Community messaging may also help mitigate potential risks and concerns. From a cost perspective, syphilis self-testing, including dual HIV/syphilis self-tests, appears to be cost-effective and affordable compared to standard laboratory-based testing. However, the cost per reactive person tested may be slightly higher due to the need for improved targeting of self-testing. Strategic use of self-tests can optimize health worker time and resources. Syphilis self-testing has the potential to improve equity by increasing access to testing for populations that may not otherwise seek testing. This approach is particularly important for reaching underserved populations and supporting global efforts to increase syphilis testing and treatment coverage. When implementing syphilis self-testing, it is essential to provide clear guidance on interpreting results and accessing confirmatory testing and treatment. Individuals with non-reactive results can be considered negative and should receive information on STI prevention. Those with reactive results should be linked to confirmatory testing and care. Programs should also prioritize the availability of penicillin for same-day treatment, particularly for pregnant women, to prevent adverse birth outcomes. Syphilis self-testing should never be coercive or mandatory. Individuals uncertain about their test results should be encouraged to seek further testing from trained health workers. Clear policies, supportive regulations, and standard training are critical to ensuring the appropriate and effective implementation of syphilis self-testing.
